definition: An open-source system that runs and manages containers for you across a whole group of machines -- deciding where each one runs, restarting it if it crashes, and scaling it up or down as load changes.
The tool that packages an app and everything it needs into a single container and runs that one container on one machine -- Kubernetes then takes many of these and orchestrates them across a cluster.

The ongoing work of deciding where each container should run, restarting it if it dies, and scaling it up or down as demand changes -- this is the job Kubernetes automates across a whole cluster, on top of Docker's job of just running one container on one machine.
The whole group of machines Kubernetes manages together as one unit -- split into a control plane that makes decisions and nodes that actually run your workloads.
The 'brain' half of a cluster: the set of components that decide what should run and where, as opposed to the nodes, which are the machines that actually run it.
One of the worker machines in a cluster that actually runs your containers, as directed by the control plane.
The single database that stores every fact about a cluster's current state -- only the API server talks to it directly, so it's the cluster's one source of truth.
The one door every request to a cluster passes through, whether it's you running kubectl or a component inside Kubernetes itself -- nothing talks to etcd directly except this.
The control-plane component that picks which node a new pod should run on, based on that pod's resource needs and any placement constraints -- you don't choose the machine yourself.
The agent that runs on every node and actually talks to the container runtime to start, stop, and keep monitoring that node's containers.

The low-level software on a node that actually creates and runs containers -- pulling images, then starting and stopping the processes inside them -- which the kubelet calls out to rather than doing itself (e.g. containerd or CRI-O).
The command-line tool you use to talk to a cluster's API server -- both to ask questions about it (like listing pods) and to tell it what state you want.
The smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers that always run together on the same node, sharing the same network address and storage.
A helper container that shares a pod with the main application container, using that same network and storage -- commonly used for things like logging or proxying traffic.
A controller that keeps a fixed number of identical pods running at all times, automatically starting a replacement if one crashes or disappears.
The controller most people actually use day to day -- it manages a ReplicaSet underneath and adds rolling updates and easy rollbacks on top of it.
Like a Deployment, but each pod gets a stable, unique identity and its own persistent storage that follows it -- the right fit for stateful apps like databases.
A controller that runs exactly one copy of a pod on every node in the cluster -- a natural fit for things like logging or monitoring agents that need to be everywhere.
A controller that runs a task to completion once, then stops -- unlike a Deployment, it isn't meant to keep running forever.
A Job that repeats on a schedule you set, like a nightly backup, instead of running just once.
An object that gives a changing set of pods one stable network address, so other things can reliably reach them even as individual pods come and go and their IPs change.
The default Service type -- gives pods a stable address that's reachable only from inside the cluster, not from the internet.
A Service type that opens the same port on every node in the cluster, making the service reachable from outside using any node's address.
A Service type that asks the cloud provider for a real external, internet-facing address -- the option for exposing something to the public internet.

Kubernetes' built-in DNS system that lets one pod reach another by a stable name -- typically a Service's name -- instead of by IP address, since a pod's IP can change whenever it restarts or moves to a different node.
An object that defines HTTP routing rules for external traffic coming into a cluster, based on things like hostname or URL path.
The component that actually reads an Ingress object's routing rules and implements them, sending real traffic where it says to.
An object that holds an app's configuration separately from its container image, so you can change a setting without rebuilding or redeploying anything.
Like a ConfigMap, but for sensitive values like passwords, tokens, and keys -- handled with more care so they don't sit in plain regular configuration.
Storage attached to a pod that outlives a single container restart -- without one, anything a container wrote to its own local disk is wiped when it restarts.
A piece of real storage that already exists and is available in the cluster, ready for a pod to claim and use.
A pod's request for storage -- separate from the PersistentVolume itself, which is the actual storage that fulfills that request.
A setup that lets Kubernetes create storage automatically the moment a claim needs it, instead of an admin having to pre-provision volumes by hand.
A logical space inside one cluster that lets different teams, environments, or projects share it without their objects colliding or interfering.
A key-value tag attached to a Kubernetes object (like a pod), used to identify and organize it -- almost every other Kubernetes feature builds on this tagging system.
A query that finds Kubernetes objects by matching the labels attached to them.
A rule that attracts a pod toward certain nodes when the scheduler places it, based on labels on those nodes.
A marker on a node that repels pods away from it, unless a pod explicitly carries a matching toleration -- the opposite effect of node affinity.
A setting on a pod that lets it ignore a specific taint and be scheduled onto that node anyway.
A recurring check that confirms a pod is still alive and working -- if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod.
A check that confirms a pod is ready to accept real traffic -- until it passes, Kubernetes won't send requests to that pod.
A check that runs before the liveness and readiness probes, giving a slow-booting app enough time to start before the other probes begin judging it.
A YAML file that describes the state you want a cluster to be in -- not a sequence of commands -- which kubectl apply then works out how to achieve.
A packaging tool that bundles a set of Kubernetes manifests into a single reusable, configurable chart, so you can install a whole app with one command instead of applying many YAML files by hand.
A reusable, configurable package of Kubernetes manifests created with Helm, used to install or upgrade a whole application in one step.
A tool that customizes plain Kubernetes YAML by layering small patches on top of a base version -- unlike Helm, it needs no templating language.
A way of deploying a new version that replaces old pods with new ones a few at a time, instead of all at once, so the app stays available with zero downtime throughout.
Undoing a rolling update and returning to the previous working version, used when a new deployment turns out to be broken.
Role-Based Access Control -- the system that grants specific cluster permissions to users or service accounts through defined roles, instead of giving everyone full access.
A cap on the total resources (like CPU and memory) a whole namespace is allowed to use, so one team can't starve out everyone else sharing the cluster.
A rule that limits how many pods of a workload can go down at once during a voluntary disruption, like planned node maintenance, protecting its overall availability.
Internet Protocol address: the number that identifies a device or pod on a network.
Internet Protocol addresses: the numbers that identify devices or pods on a network.
A human-readable text format for configuration, used for Kubernetes manifests.
Central processing unit: the processor that executes a program's instructions.
Domain Name System: the service that turns names into IP addresses.
The DNS server that runs inside a Kubernetes cluster so pods and Services can find each other by name.
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes pods automatically as load changes.
Kubernetes objects that hold non-secret configuration for pods.
PersistentVolume: a piece of storage in the cluster that outlives any one pod.
PersistentVolumeClaim: a pod's request for storage from a PersistentVolume.
Kubernetes objects that run pods needing stable names and their own storage.
Kubernetes objects that run one copy of a pod on every node.
Kubernetes objects that keep a set number of identical pods running.
Kubernetes objects that run a Job on a repeating schedule.
Kubernetes objects that cap how many resources a namespace may use.
PodDisruptionBudget: a limit on how many pods of an app may be down at once during planned maintenance.
PodDisruptionBudgets: limits on how many pods of an app may be down at once during planned maintenance.
Kubernetes objects that give a user or service account the permissions of a Role.
HyperText Transfer Protocol: the protocol web browsers and servers use to exchange pages and data.
HTTP carried over an encrypted connection.
Media access control address: the hardware address of a network card.
Uniform resource identifier: a string that names a resource, such as a web address.
Layer 7: the application layer of the network stack, where HTTP lives.
A file that explains what a project is and how to use it.
User interfaces: the screens and controls people use to work with software.
Comma-separated values: a plain-text table format where each line is a row.
Groups of machines that Kubernetes manages together as one system.
The Kubernetes components that decide where pods run and keep the cluster in its desired state.
The worker machines in a Kubernetes cluster where pods actually run.
The smallest deployable units in Kubernetes: one or more containers sharing network and storage.
Kubernetes objects that keep a set number of identical pods running and roll out updates.
Kubernetes objects that give a set of pods one stable address and load-balance across them.
Kubernetes objects that hold sensitive data such as passwords and tokens.
Storage attached to a pod that can outlive individual containers.
Named partitions that divide one cluster into separate virtual areas.
Attaching key-value tags to Kubernetes objects so they can be grouped and selected.
Key-value tags attached to Kubernetes objects so they can be grouped and selected.
Queries that pick Kubernetes objects by their labels.
Marks on a node that repel pods unless the pod tolerates them.
Settings on a pod that let it be scheduled onto nodes with matching taints.
Health checks that tell Kubernetes when a container is ready to receive traffic.
YAML files that describe the Kubernetes objects you want to exist.
Updates that replace pods a few at a time so the app stays available.
Returning a Deployment to a previous working version after a bad update.
